title: Leyner Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Leyner wells have a 56-foot median depth, but records range to 1,400 feet. See yields, water levels, drilling costs and local risks.
h1: Leyner, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Leyner means looking past the listing and into the well record. Within 5 miles, Colorado Division of Water Resources records include 2,962 permitted wells. Of those, 1,733 are recorded as constructed, 1,900 report a total depth, 346 report a pump yield, and 91 report a static water level.

The local numbers are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. A well near Gunbarrel, Erie, Lafayette, Niwot, or Valmont may be completed in different material and under a different permit. Neighboring wells are still the best first check before you buy or design a house.

sections.heading: Leyner well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Leyner is 56 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 205 feet, meaning half of the wells with reported depths fall inside that range. The 90th percentile is 325 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,400 feet.

Depths are spread unevenly. Fifty-six percent of records are under 100 feet, 29% are between 100 and 300 feet, 14% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% are 600 feet or deeper. That spread matters when you request a bid: a median-depth estimate may be reasonable for a first budget, but a driller still needs to account for the specific formation, access, casing, grout, and the chance that the well must go deeper.

Permits identify 82% of the wells with Denver Basin aquifers. Other records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, Alluvial water, or Laramie Fox Hills.

sections.heading: Most Leyner wells make usable flow, but records are limited
sections.html:
Among the 346 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls from 9.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-nine percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 31% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low production is present but not common in the reported sample: 2% are under 1 gallon per minute and 8% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A buyer should not treat the median as a promise. The well test, storage tank, pump setting, household demand, and permit conditions all affect how much water is practically available.

Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. A higher reported yield does not automatically mean the property can use that flow for irrigation or additional buildings. Confirm the permit and allowed uses with DWR before relying on the number.

sections.heading: Leyner water levels do not show a simple one-way decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are relatively shallow overall. The median depth to water is 14 feet, with the middle half from 9 to 27 feet below the surface. That can simplify pumping compared with a very deep water level, but it also means surface activities and construction practices deserve attention.

The decade figures do not establish a clean long-term decline. Median static water level was 20 feet in the 1960s, 25 feet in the 1970s, 35 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. The 2010s value was deeper than the earlier measurements, while the 2020s value was shallower.

These measurements come from only 91 records and may represent different wells, locations, and conditions. For a purchase, compare the target well's current water level and production test with nearby permits rather than using the decade series alone.

sections.heading: Permit activity runs from older wells to a 2026 record
sections.html:
Leyner has a long permit history. Records show 82 permits from the 1950s, 110 from the 1960s, 408 from the 1970s, 240 from the 1980s, 329 from the 1990s, 260 from the 2000s, 346 from the 2010s, and 278 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026.

The most frequently listed driller is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 514 records. Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don) appears on 316, and Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) appears on 132.

Those names describe the permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available for your project. Before closing, pull the actual permit, construction report, pump information, and any abandonment record for the target parcel. An old permit may not describe current equipment or current water quality.

sections.heading: A Leyner well budget starts with depth, then adds the system
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 56-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,800 to $3,900. That is only the drilling portion.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $8,800 to $15,900 at that median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole can move the price well beyond that starting range, especially when access, casing, grout, difficult drilling, or additional site work is involved.

Ask bidders to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, tank, electrical, trenching, permits, testing, and any water-treatment work. On a rural lot, the cheapest drilling number is not necessarily the lowest complete project cost. Confirm what happens if the first hole has inadequate production or must be deepened.

sections.heading: Before building near Leyner, check water, waste, and the lot
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one risk. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 705 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 103 historic mine features, and 23 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular property, but they are a reason to test the actual well and understand the local site history.

Low-yield wells and dry holes remain possible even where nearby records look favorable. Fractured-bedrock conditions can change over short distances. Ask for the well construction report, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and maintenance history. Check neighboring wells near the parcel, not just a countywide average.

Before placing a house, septic system, driveway, or irrigation area, verify setbacks, drainage, access for a drilling rig, and the well permit's allowed use. An augmentation plan may be required in an over-appropriated basin. Confirm the building and septic layout before spending money on plans.

sections.heading: A practical purchase plan for a Leyner lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's permit number and locate the well on the ground. Compare its reported depth and production with nearby records in Leyner and surrounding areas such as Gunbarrel, Erie, Lafayette, Niwot, and Valmont. The local median yield is encouraging, but the relatively small number of yield reports means the target well's own test matters more.

For an existing home, make the contract review include the well permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality test, storage and pressure equipment, and septic records. For vacant land, get a driller's site review and a written estimate that identifies the assumed depth and what is excluded.

Do not design the house or septic field until access, setbacks, drainage, and water availability are confirmed. If the permitted use does not match your plans, resolve that with DWR before closing. A well that produces water is not automatically approved for every intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Leyner, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Leyner is 56 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 205 feet, but the 90th percentile is 325 feet and the deepest record is 1,400 feet. Local conditions vary, particularly where permits identify fractured bedrock or different Denver Basin formations.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Leyner?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 56-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800 to $3,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,800 to $15,900. Greater depth, access, casing, grout, and difficult ground can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Leyner wells produce?
faq.a: Among 346 records with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-nine percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% are under 1 gallon per minute, but the target well's own test is more useful than the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Leyner?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every Leyner well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped information includes 705 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 103 historic mine features, and 23 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for relevant contaminants and review its construction, nearby land uses, and maintenance history.

faq.q: Do Leyner wells have enough water for a new home?
faq.a: Many reported wells produce useful flow, with a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median, but production varies. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and permit conditions control allowed uses. Confirm the target permit, pump test, storage, septic layout, and any augmentation-plan requirement before assuming water is available for a home or irrigation.
